paragraphs:
Shimon ben Shetah, the nasi; his colleague Yehudah ben Tabbai was head of the court: Mishnah, Ein Doreshin, 16a. He is also mentioned in Mishnah Ta'anit, chapter 3, mishnah 8. His sister was married to King Yannai of the Hasmoneans: Berakhot 48a. Three hundred nazirites came up in his days. Each nazirite needs three offerings: a ewe for a sin-offering, a male lamb for a burnt-offering, and a ram for a peace-offering. For a hundred and fifty he found a ground for releasing them, and for a hundred and fifty he did not. He came to Yannai and said, “There are three hundred nazirites here who need nine hundred offerings. You give half, and I shall give half.” He sent him four hundred and fifty. They spoke slander, saying that he had given nothing of his own. Yannai heard and became angry; Shimon ben Shetah fled. Afterward he sent for him, and so forth: Jerusalem Sheloshah she-Akhelu, mishnah 2; Nazir, end of Beit Shammai. The end of the matter is in the Bavli, the foregoing Sheloshah she-Akhelu. See Bereshit Rabbah, chapter 91, and Midrash Kohelet, at “Wisdom is good with an inheritance.” In Sifra, Behukkotai: in his days and the days of Queen Shalmatzi, rains fell from Sabbath eve to Sabbath eve, and the wheat grew as large as kidneys. The sages tied up samples for future generations, to show how much sin causes. So too in Ta'anit, chapter 3, 23b. Queen Shaltzion held a banquet for her son, and her utensils became impure. She broke them and gave them to the metalworker. Rashi explains that it was in Shimon ben Shetah's days: Shabbat 16b. Tosafot write: as in Ta'anit, in the days of Shimon ben Shetah and Queen Shaltzion, rains fell, and so forth. In the foregoing Kohelet Rabbah, he said to Shalmati, his sister, Yannai's wife. Thus one may say that there is a scribal error between Shalmati and Shaltzion. In Vayikra Rabbah, chapter 35: Queen Shaltzmah.

He enacted ordinances: Shabbat, first chapter, 14b, and elsewhere. He enacted for the marriage contract that all the husband's property be liable. In Mishnah Nigmar ha-Din: he hanged eighty women who practiced witchcraft on one day. Rashi there says that two people testified against his son, who was sentenced to death. The witnesses recanted and said that because he had hanged the witches, they had testified falsely. Nevertheless, he was not released, because his son in his piety said that judgment should be carried out on him and Torah law should not be undermined. See Jerusalem Nigmar ha-Din, halakhah 9, and Ahad Dinei Mamonot, halakhah 2, for the matter at length. In Ahad Dinei Mamonot, 37b: he saw someone running after another, ran after him, and saw a sword in his hand, blood dripping from it, and the slain man convulsing. He said, “Wicked man! Who killed this person—I or you? But your blood is not entrusted to my hand. He who knows thoughts will exact payment from that man who killed his fellow.” They did not move from there before a snake bit him and he died. In Sanhedrin 19a: King Yannai's slave killed a person. They sent to him that the king should come and stand, for testimony to be received in his presence. He came and sat. Shimon ben Shetah said to him, “Stand on your feet, and they shall testify concerning you ….” Yannai answered, “Not as you say, but as your colleagues say.” He turned right; they lowered their faces to the ground. Likewise to his left. Shimon ben Shetah said, “Let the Master of thoughts come and exact payment from you.” Immediately Gavriel came, struck them down to the ground, and they died.

He worked in gallnuts. His pupils bought him a donkey from an Ishmaelite, and a pearl was hanging on it. He returned it for the sanctification of the Lord. The gentile said, “Blessed is the God of Shimon ben Shetah”: Jerusalem Ellu Metzi'ot, halakhah 5; and Rabbah, Ekev. Honi the Circle-Drawer lived in his time. R' Yehudah ben Dostai reports in his name. R' Yehoshua ben Perahyah was his teacher. Shemayah and Avtalyon were his pupils. Todos. (Nahalat Shimoni did not arrange him according to the generations.)
